newsitem.title: CROATIA: Top E.Euro currencies should fix to mark-economist.
newsitem.headline: Top E.Euro currencies should fix to mark-economist.

text.p: East Europe's most advanced economies should fix their currencies to the mark in preparation for European economic and monetary union (EMU), a leading economist said on Thursday.

The Czech Republic, Slovakia, Slovenia and Croatia should fix to the mark to be ready for the monetary policies of EMU but backed by currency boards, said Robert Mundell of New York's Columbia University.

"The euro will not be as disinflationary or anti-inflationary as the mark but it will be a much better European currency," he told a conference on transition economies. "The euro is going to be a plus for moving to a fixing," he said.
Mundell said a fix to the mark would be the third and final stage for post-communist economies which would require economic fundamentals to be in order.
For countries at the first stage, which include Russia and several former Soviet republics, the key task was to reduce the rate of money supply growth and achieve fiscal balance.

Stage two, at which Mundell placed Poland, Hungary, Lithuania, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia, the target should be cutting inflation below five percent. The Transcaucasus republics should prepare to fix to the dollar, the others to the mark once inflation was brought down.
Mundell told the conference that pegging to the mark would give countries cheaper access to capital.
Many emerging east European currencies shadow the mark in a more or less formal way.
Hungary operates a crawling peg system against a mark/dollar basket, Poland against five Western currencies. The Sovak crown is fixed in a plus/minus seven percent band against a dollar/mark basket

But the debate about whether to have a fixed or floating currency, particularly in coutries with big current account deficits and high capital inflows, has been highlighted by the recent troubles of the Czech crown.
The central bank was forced to float the crown in late May after massive speculative selling by investors alarmed at widening trade and current account deficits and growing political uncertainty.
The central bank scrapped the bands within which the crown was fixed against a mark/dollar basket in favour of a managed float in which the mark rate is the key.

Mundell said that despite their recent troubles, the Czechs should still fix. "It would be a good policy. What they would gain from it is integration with the German capital markets," he told Reuters at the confernce, held in the historic Croatian port city of Dubrovnik.
However, some policy-makers at the conference were wary about pegging to the mark.

Velimir Bole of Ljubljana's Economic Institute, and a member of the central bank board, said it was not realistic to fix the Slovenian tolar as real wage growth of four perent a year was still too high.
"If the fundamentals are not in place, then I think monetary anchoring is better," he told Reuters.

Croatian Deputy Prime Minister Borislav Skegro said that in adopting pro-market policies, many east European countries had chosen flexibilty in exchange rates in place of the former rigidity of the socialist system.
He also saw political difficulties in a fix to the mark when it is scheduled to disappear by 1999.
Many Croatians held their savings in marks, he said, and added: "I do not think people will say the euro is as good as the Deutschemark."
In fact the Croatian kuna has been very stable against the mark. It stood at 3.7 in May 1994 when it was introduced and now trades at about 3.56, Skegro said.
